passage:
Mahima had been hurt at Sharmila's birthday dinner in Kolkata, when Sharmila laughed at her job-interview story and said, "Only you would wear that to an interview." Everyone laughed. Mahima laughed too, then went quiet.
After that she said "maybe" to the Sunday adda and didn't come. She took longer to reply in the group chat. When Sharmila called, she let it ring and texted later, "Busy with assignments!" It felt easier than saying, "That comment stung."
Weeks passed. The hurt didn't fade; it hardened. One evening Mahima saw photos of the group at their usual café, Sharmila in the middle, and felt a sharp ache. The friendship was drifting, and she had never even told Sharmila why.

qa.q: What did Sharmila say at the birthday dinner?
qa.a: "Only you would wear that to an interview."

qa.q: Why did going quiet feel easier to Mahima than speaking up?
qa.a: Saying 'That comment stung' felt awkward and risky, so avoiding Sharmila gave quick relief, even though the hurt kept hardening.

qa.q: What could Mahima do now that the friendship is drifting?
qa.a: Call Sharmila and say calmly that the interview comment hurt and that she has missed the group, giving the friendship a chance to be repaired.

qa.q: How might Sharmila experience Mahima's slow replies and missed addas?
qa.a: Confused and perhaps hurt, not knowing the joke was the reason and wondering what went wrong.

grounding: A young woman hurt by a friend's joke goes quiet and skips plans instead of saying so, and the friendship drifts.

subtype: Dodging a hard talk with a friend [Actor]
passage:
Outside the college library:
"Hansa! Finally. You've skipped three movie nights."
"Assignments."
"You answered my message with a thumbs-up. Just a thumbs-up. After I sent a whole paragraph."
"I was busy, Arohi."
"You weren't too busy for the drama club lot at the canteen."
"...Okay."
"Did I do something?"
Hansa looked at the notice board. It would be so easy to say "no, nothing". It had been easy for two weeks.
"...You told everyone about my scholarship rejection. At the hostel dinner. I told you that in private."
Arohi's face fell. "Oh. Hansa, I thought I was being supportive. I'm so sorry. Why didn't you tell me?"
"I thought it'd go away if I just stayed out of your way."
"Did it?"
"No. It got worse."

qa.q: How many movie nights had Hansa skipped?
qa.a: Three movie nights.

qa.q: Why had Hansa stayed quiet for two weeks instead of telling Arohi?
qa.a: Hansa hoped the hurt would go away by keeping out of Arohi's way, which felt easier than a hard conversation.

qa.q: What turning point finally opened the real conversation?
qa.a: Arohi asking directly, 'Did I do something?', and Hansa choosing, for once, not to say 'no, nothing'.

qa.q: How does Arohi seem to feel on learning the reason?
qa.a: Shocked and sorry, having thought the sharing was supportive, and sad the friendship had been drifting without Arohi knowing why.

grounding: A student hurt by a friend's broken confidence avoids the friend for weeks, until a direct question brings the real reason out.

subtype: Dodging a hard talk with a friend [Actor]
passage:
In second year, Pranav said something at a party that stuck in me like a splinter. I'd told him I was thinking of switching to design, and he said loudly, "Ishita wants to draw pictures for a living?" People laughed. He probably forgot by morning. I didn't. But I didn't tell him either.
I just started saying no. No to the Friday chai. No to the road trip. I left the study group. I told myself it would fade if I didn't poke at it. It didn't fade. It grew, and our friendship shrank around it.
By the time I finally mentioned it, months later, he was hurt and baffled. "Why didn't you just say?" he asked. "I'd have apologised that night." He did apologise. But we had lost most of a year.

qa.q: What did Pranav say at the party?
qa.a: "Ishita wants to draw pictures for a living?"

qa.q: Why did Ishita start saying no instead of telling Pranav?
qa.a: Ishita hoped the hurt would fade without a hard conversation, and avoiding him gave short-term relief.

qa.q: What turning point showed Ishita what the avoidance had cost?
qa.a: Finally mentioning it and hearing Pranav say he'd have apologised that night, which showed that most of a year had been lost for nothing.

qa.q: What might Pranav have felt during those months of refusals?
qa.a: Confused and slowly pushed away, with no idea his joke had caused it.

grounding: A young adult hurt by a friend's joke avoids him for months instead of talking, and later sees how much the silence cost.

subtype: Dodging a hard talk with a friend [Actor]
passage:
Coach's note, college badminton club, 14 August

Mehak has missed four evening sessions in a row. She was never a skipper. When I called, she said, "Exams, sir," but her friend and doubles partner Sonali says Mehak's exams are next month.

Today Mehak came to return the club shuttle tube. I asked her plainly if something had happened. After a long pause she said Sonali had joked, in front of the whole team, that Mehak "only won because of the partner". Everyone laughed. Mehak laughed too, then went home and hasn't really come back since. "I'll just stay away for a bit. It'll pass," she said. She looked relieved just saying it.

I think it may not pass by itself. Sonali seems puzzled, not unkind; she asked me if Mehak was angry with her.

Next step: I've offered Mehak my office on Friday if she wants to speak to Sonali with someone nearby.

qa.q: How many evening sessions has Mehak missed in a row?
qa.a: Mehak has missed four evening sessions in a row.

qa.q: Why did Mehak look relieved when she said "It'll pass"?
qa.a: Staying away means she doesn't have to face the hurt or risk an awkward talk with Sonali. Just deciding not to deal with it brought a quick sense of relief.

qa.q: What is the turning point the coach is trying to create for Mehak?
qa.a: The chance to tell Sonali directly how the joke landed, in a calm place with support. That choice, instead of more distance, gives the friendship a chance to be repaired.

qa.q: How does Sonali seem to see Mehak's absence?
qa.a: Sonali seems puzzled, not unkind, and even asks the coach if Mehak is angry. Sonali may not know the joke hurt, so the silence leaves Sonali guessing.

grounding: A coach notices a young woman quietly withdrawing after a friend's hurtful joke, hoping it will pass, while the friendship loses its chance to be mended.

subtype: Dodging a hard talk with a friend [Actor]
passage:
Saturday, late

Didn't go to cricket at the maidan today. Told the group I had a headache. I didn't.

It's still the thing Yogesh said on Wednesday, when I told everyone about my internship interview. "Arre, they take anyone these days." He laughed. Everyone laughed. I smiled and changed the subject, and then my face was hot all the way home on the local.

Since then I've been answering the group chat with one word. I skipped Thursday's chai. Today, cricket. Every time I skip, I feel lighter for an hour. Then I see photos, Yogesh with the bat, and something in my chest goes tight.

I keep thinking: he probably didn't mean it. It'll just wear off. But it hasn't worn off, and I'm the one missing Saturday.

Maybe I just say, "That comment hurt." Four words. Why does that feel harder than missing everything?

— Swati

qa.q: What excuse did Swati give the group for missing cricket?
qa.a: Swati told the group about a headache that wasn't real.

qa.q: What does the tightness in Swati's chest, on seeing the photos, suggest Swati is feeling?
qa.a: Swati seems to miss the friends and feel left out, and the hurt from Yogesh's comment is still there. Staying away has brought a short lift but not real peace.

qa.q: What small step would help Swati more than skipping another Saturday?
qa.a: Telling Yogesh privately, in a few words, that the comment hurt. It gives him a chance to apologise, which the silence never will.

qa.q: How might Yogesh and the group see Swati's one-word replies and missed plans?
qa.a: They may think Swati is busy or has lost interest, not that Swati is hurt. Yogesh, not knowing, can't fix anything.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows quiet withdrawal from friends after a hurtful remark, getting brief relief while the friendship drifts.
